summary: Documents how DNS-based blacklists and whitelists work: lists of IP addresses or domains, mostly used to fight spam, that are distributed and queried through the DNS. It describes the structure of these lists and the query protocol. It is informational, recording existing practice.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS blacklists and whitelists let a service ask DNS whether an IP address or domain appears on a shared list. RFC 5782 describes how the records are formed, queried, and checked.

questions: how to check if an ip is blacklisted
how do you check if an ip is listed
subtitle: How DNS-based lists publish and answer queries about IP addresses and domains.

tldr.problem: Network operators wanted to share lists of IP addresses and domains associated with unwanted or preferred traffic, without distributing them only as routing feeds.
tldr.mechanism: DNS-based blacklists and whitelists publish entries as DNS records. A client constructs a query name from an address or domain and interprets the returned records as list information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5782 documents the structure and use of existing DNS-based lists. It does not prescribe list-management policies or how operators must use them.

today: RFC 5782 is an Informational IRTF document and the supplied metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: What DNS-Based Lists Do
sections.content:
A DNS blacklist (DNSBL) lists IP addresses or domains, often for use in deciding whether to accept traffic. A DNS whitelist (DNSWL) lists entries that an operator may prefer to accept. The RFC uses DNSxL to refer to either kind of list.

The DNS carries these lists as zones that clients query using DNS. The document describes their structure and use for interoperability; it does not recommend policies for adding or removing entries or for applying list results.
sections.plainLanguage: A DNSBL or DNSWL is a list published through DNS. A service can query a list for an address instead of downloading the whole list.

sections.title: How Queries Name an Entry
sections.content:
For an IPv4 list, the query name reverses the address's octets and appends the list's domain. For example, 192.0.2.99 becomes 99.2.0.192.bad.example.com when the list domain is bad.example.com. Each listed entry must have an A record; a TXT record may explain why it is listed.

IPv6 list names reverse the address's hexadecimal nibbles. A domain-name list puts the listed domain before the list domain. The A-record value is a list code, not an address to use for connecting to the listed host.
sections.plainLanguage: The query name encodes the address or domain and adds the list's own domain. An answer means the entry is listed; the A-record value carries list meaning, not the listed host's address.

sections.title: Typical Queries and Cache Behavior
sections.content:
A mail server may query DNSBLs when an SMTP connection arrives. A returned A record means the entry is listed; no record means it is not listed. An operator may reject a connection based on a list, accept it based on a whitelist, or use list results as inputs to a scoring system.

DNS caches can reduce repeated queries. A client that keeps its own cache must respect the record's time to live and discard expired data. List operators choose TTL and refresh intervals to reflect how quickly their entries are expected to change.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail server can query a list when a connection arrives and use the answer in its own decision. Cached results must expire according to the DNS TTL.

sections.title: Test Entries and Risks
sections.content:
An IPv4 DNSxL must contain a test entry for 127.0.0.2 and must not contain one for 127.0.0.1. These checks help a client detect a zone that is not a valid list or that has been changed to return a wildcard answer. IPv6 lists have corresponding IPv4-mapped IPv6 test entries.

Operators trust list managers to apply suitable policies, and a poorly chosen list can block wanted traffic. DNSxL queries also reveal query activity to the list operator and remain subject to ordinary DNS attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients can use required test entries to check that a DNS domain still behaves like a list. Operators should choose lists whose policies match their own, because a list can affect which traffic they accept.
